Subject: Evaluating long-haul connectivity for Private deployment

Vanessa,

Thanks again for onboarding time today — quick follow-up from our infra team. We're trying to settle on a path for connecting our primary data center (east-us-2) to Redwood Private. Our three options right now: VPC peering (cross-account peering), PrivateLink-like interface endpoints, or a site-to-site IPsec tunnel to a small egress appliance.

Key constraints:
- We need end-to-end TLS + mTLS for control plane traffic; audit logs must be delivered to our SIEM.
- Per-req latency target: 20–40ms p95 for inference RPCs between our app tier and Redwood.
- We want predictable throughput (1.5–2 Gbps sustained) and graceful fallback to a cheaper path if cost spikes.
- Our networking folks prefer minimal public exposure and simple IAM scoping.

Can you share a short comparative recommendation with operational tradeoffs? Also attaching a sketch of our proposed overlay.

—Sanjay

Hi Sanjay — Markus (infra) here. Short technical breakdown based on your constraints. I included example operational checks you can use in a checklist.

1) VPC peering (cross-account peering)
- Pros: lowest network hop count inside cloud provider backbone; minimal proxying; predictable low latency if both VPCs are in-region or connected via provider backbone. Easy to test with perf runs.
- Cons: cross-account peering requires careful route table management and explicit CIDR planning. No private endpoint abstraction — the other side must expose an IP/range. Billing: egress/ingress depends on provider (some inter-AZ costs). Scaling: adding more peering connections for multi-region gets operationally complex.
- Operational checklist: route table audit, IAM controls for accept/modify peering, flow logs -> SIEM integration, test perf baseline (iperf/tcp ping).

2) Interface endpoints (PrivateLink-style)
- Pros: fine-grained access control (service-level), supports endpoint policies (ACLs) and cross-account service exposure without exposing whole VPC. Simplifies limiting surface area and aligns with least-privilege. Can terminate TLS at your side or handshake to Redwood with mTLS.
- Cons: additional network hop to endpoint appliances; potential throughput limits on individual endpoint ENIs (need to verify quotas); cost model often includes per-hour and per-GB charges. Latency often slightly higher than peering but more stable for multi-tenant exposures.
- Operational checklist: verify endpoint throughput quotas, sigterm/mTLS cipher suites, per-endpoint logging (ENI flow logs), accelerate with placement groups if available.

3) Site-to-site VPN (IPsec appliance at your DC -> Redwood edge)
- Pros: lowest friction for on-prem environments; full control over egress appliances; you can route specific subnets to Redwood. Good for hybrid setups and when you need on-prem to cloud fallbacks.
- Cons: higher tail latency and less predictable p95 due to public internet or transit SP variability unless you use dedicated circuits (MPLS/Direct Connect style). Operationally heavier: manage key rotation, HA for appliances, and monitoring for tunnel flaps. Throughput often limited by appliance and public link capacity (but can be scaled with multiple tunnels/aggregation).
- Operational checklist: BFD/tunnel monitoring, symmetric routing verification, MTU/path-MTU testing, IPsec cipher and IKE v2 config, failover plan to alternate route, SIEM collection for logs.

Recommendation (given your 20–40ms p95 and 1.5–2 Gbps target):
- If both endpoints are in the same cloud region and you can accept cross-account peering: VPC peering offers the best latency and simplest throughput scaling. Ensure CIDR hygiene and route control.
- If you need strict surface-area reduction, per-service policies, or your security team requires no broad network exposure: go with PrivateLink (interface endpoints) but run a performance test to validate p95 — may see +5–15ms overhead in practice. Also plan for endpoint throughput quotas and potentially multiple ENIs to hit your bandwidth targets.
- If your data center must remain the source of truth (on-prem-only), start with IPsec S2S but plan a migration to peering or PrivateLink for production SLAs; use dedicated circuits for stable latency if budget permits.

I'll attach a short tech brief that lists cipher examples and a perf-run playbook. Happy to jump on a quick call with your netops folks.

Sanjay — adding commercial/provisioning notes so you can see the timeline and cost implications.

- VPC peering: Quickest to provision if both accounts are cloud-native; minimal ongoing fees beyond normal egress. Timeline: 1–3 business days for peering setup + route approvals (we can assist with a route-change template).
- PrivateLink (interface endpoints): Longer lead due to quota checks and endpoint creation, plus per-hour/per-GB charges. Timeline: ~3–10 business days depending on quota requests. We typically recommend creating an endpoint per AZ to avoid single-ENI bottlenecks.
- S2S VPN: Fast to stand up for PoC (1–5 days) but expect 2–4 weeks for hardened HA topology and runbooks. If you want a resilient production link we recommend dual tunnels and BGP for dynamic failover.

Next steps (M.A.P. draft):
1) DataHarbor NetOps to confirm CIDRs to publish and desired NAT behavior (due: 2027-06-14)
2) Redwood to run a peering perf test in a staging account (due: 2027-06-16) — contact: markus.klein@redwood.com
3) If peering fails perf threshold, Redwood to provision PrivateLink test endpoints and run perf baseline (due: 2027-06-18)
4) Procurement/Legal: define SLA uplift and ingress egress charges (by DH procurement, due: 2027-06-25)

I've attached the MAP spreadsheet and a short pricing sketch. If useful, Vanessa can schedule a 30-min netops call.
